---
title: "Monte Carlo integration and importance sampling"
subtitle: "Lecture 3"
---

## Overview

By the end of this lecture you can compute any posterior summary for a model that
has no closed form, and state how accurate your answer is.

::: {.callout-important}
## The result of this chapter

For independent draws $\theta^{(1)}, \dots, \theta^{(S)}$ from a distribution $p$
and any function $g$ with finite variance $\sigma_g^2$ under $p$,

$$
\hat g_S = \frac{1}{S}\sum_{s=1}^{S} g\big(\theta^{(s)}\big),
\qquad
\mathbb{E}\big[\hat g_S\big] = \mathbb{E}_p[g(\theta)],
\qquad
\text{MCSE} = \frac{\sigma_g}{\sqrt{S}},
$$

so any expectation under a distribution we can draw from is an average, unbiased,
and carrying its own error estimate whatever the dimension of $\theta$. Two
difficulties remain, and the rest of the chapter is about them: the error falls
only at rate $S^{-1/2}$, and a posterior is almost never a distribution we can
draw from directly.
:::

After working through this chapter you can

1. derive the mean, variance and limiting distribution of the Monte Carlo
   estimator, and report its standard error alongside every simulated number;
2. diagnose why a posterior without conjugate structure admits no closed-form
   summary, and why deterministic quadrature stops being an option as $k$ grows;
3. derive the importance sampling identity and its self-normalised estimator, and
   say where the bias comes from and how fast it vanishes;
4. implement importance sampling and rejection sampling for a posterior known only
   through a kernel, and verify each against an independent reference;
5. interpret an effective sample size and a weight histogram, and decide from them
   whether a simulated estimate can be believed;
6. compute a predictive value at risk that integrates over parameter uncertainty,
   and compare it with the plug-in and Normal conventions.

Week 3 of 15, paired with the [Week 3 exercise
session](../exercise-sessions/03-monte-carlo-importance-sampling.qmd). The chapter
assumes the conjugate regression of Lecture 2, in particular its inverse-Gamma
parameterisation and its noninformative limit, and nothing from later chapters.

## Motivation: what a Normal model says about October 2008 {#sec-motivation}

A risk officer has to say how much the US equity market might lose next month, and
a strategist in the next room has to say how large the equity premium is. Both
questions are asked of the same series, the monthly excess return on the market
portfolio, and they differ only in which part of its distribution they care about:
the strategist wants the centre, the risk officer the far left tail. Both are
usually answered with a sample average and a sample standard deviation, and Lecture
2 appears to have answered them already. A regression with a
constant as its only regressor is exactly the model of @sec-methodology of that
chapter with $k = 1$, so under the noninformative limit the premium has a Student
$t$ posterior centred at the sample mean and the variance an inverse-Gamma
posterior, both in closed form and both available without a line of simulation.

The trouble is not the algebra but the assumption underneath it. Lecture 2 assumed
the errors were Normal, and the computation below asks what that assumption commits
us to.

```{python}
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from scipy import stats, optimize
from scipy.special import gammaln
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

DATA = next(p for p in (Path("data"), Path("../data")) if p.exists())

rng = np.random.default_rng(2026)
plt.rcParams.update({"figure.figsize": (7, 4.2), "axes.grid": True,
                     "grid.alpha": 0.3, "font.size": 11})

ff_m = pd.read_parquet(DATA / "ff_factors_monthly.parquet")
sample = ff_m["1990-01":"2026-07"]
r = sample["mkt_rf"].to_numpy()
n = r.size

ssr_0 = ((r - r.mean()) ** 2).sum()           # Lecture 2 with X = a column of ones
s2_0 = ssr_0 / (n - 1)
mu_post = stats.t(df=n - 1, loc=r.mean(), scale=np.sqrt(s2_0 / n))
worst = np.sort(r)[:4]
p_worst = stats.norm(r.mean(), np.sqrt(s2_0)).cdf(worst[0])

print(f"Lecture 2 posterior for the monthly premium: mean {mu_post.mean():.5f}, "
      f"95% [{mu_post.ppf(0.025):.5f}, {mu_post.ppf(0.975):.5f}]")
print(f"posterior mean of sigma^2 {ssr_0/2/((n-1)/2 - 1):.6f}, "
      f"residual sd {np.sqrt(s2_0):.5f}")
print(f"four worst months: {worst.round(3)}")
print(f"Normal probability of a month at or below {worst[0]:.3f}: {p_worst:.3e}")
print(f"that is one month in {1/p_worst:,.0f}, i.e. one in {1/p_worst/12:,.0f} years")
print(f"expected months below -10% in {n} months: {n*stats.norm(r.mean(), np.sqrt(s2_0)).cdf(-0.10):.2f}"
      f"   observed: {(r < -0.10).sum()}")

z = np.sort((r - r.mean()) / np.sqrt(s2_0))
qq = stats.norm.ppf((np.arange(1, n + 1) - 0.5) / n)
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.scatter(qq, z, s=12, alpha=0.6, color="steelblue")
ax.plot([-3.5, 3.5], [-3.5, 3.5], "k--", lw=1.2, label="Normal reference line")
ax.set_xlabel("Normal quantile"); ax.set_ylabel("standardised monthly excess return")
ax.legend(fontsize=9); ax.set_title("Where the Normal model fails: both tails")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

The closed form works perfectly. It says the monthly premium is $0.745\%$ with a
ninety-five percent credible interval from $0.333\%$ to $1.157\%$, and the residual
standard deviation is $4.39\%$ a month, all of it read off a Student $t$ and an
inverse-Gamma with no simulation anywhere. If the question were only how large the
premium is, the chapter could stop here.

The risk officer's question is the one that breaks it. What the same model says
about the worst month in the sample, a loss of $17.2\%$, is that it is a draw from
the far left of a Normal density: its probability is $2.2\times10^{-5}$, one month
in about forty-five thousand, or one in roughly three thousand eight hundred years.
Told that, a risk officer has been informed that October 2008 will not happen again
in the lifetime of the firm, which is not a statement anyone in the room believes.
The failure is systematic rather than a single unlucky month. Across the whole
sample the model expects $3.17$ months below minus ten percent and there are eight,
two and a half times as many, and the figure makes the same point without any
distributional arithmetic: the points bend away from the reference line at both
ends, so the observed extremes are larger in magnitude than a Normal with this
variance produces, while the middle of the distribution is too peaked. Over this
window the monthly excess return has a skewness of $-0.55$ and a kurtosis of $4.03$
against the Normal's $3$.

The diagnosis matters for what is repaired. Nothing here says the conjugate update
of Lecture 2 was computed wrongly, and nothing says the premium of $0.745\%$ is far
out. What is wrong is the shape of the assumed error distribution, and the
quantities most damaged by it are exactly the tail quantities a risk desk reports.
The standard repair is to let the returns be Student $t$ rather than Normal,

$$
r_t \mid \mu, \sigma, \nu \;\overset{\text{iid}}{\sim}\; t_\nu(\mu, \sigma),
\qquad
f(r_t \mid \mu, \sigma, \nu) =
\frac{\Gamma\!\big(\tfrac{\nu+1}{2}\big)}{\Gamma\!\big(\tfrac{\nu}{2}\big)\sqrt{\pi\nu}\,\sigma}
\left[1 + \frac{1}{\nu}\left(\frac{r_t - \mu}{\sigma}\right)^{\!2}\right]^{-(\nu+1)/2},
$$

which adds a third parameter, the degrees of freedom $\nu$, controlling tail
thickness. Small $\nu$ makes crashes a regular feature of the series, while $\nu$
above about thirty is indistinguishable from a Normal at this sample size. Fixing it
in advance would be assuming the answer, since how thick the tails are is precisely
what the risk officer is asking, so $\nu$ has to be an unknown with a prior and a
posterior like any other, and the natural first question of the chapter becomes how
much posterior mass sits at the small values.

That single change breaks every closed form the course has relied on so far. The next
section states the model with its priors and shows exactly what is lost, which is not
a convenience but the ability to write down any reported number at all.

## The problem: no conjugate structure, and a grid that dies with $k$ {#sec-problem}

Write $\theta = (\mu, \sigma, \nu)$, so $k = 3$, with $\mu$ the monthly equity
premium and $\sigma$ the scale, so that the return standard deviation is
$\sigma\sqrt{\nu/(\nu-2)}$ whenever $\nu > 2$. The priors are

$$
\mu \sim \mathcal{N}(m_0, s_0^2), \qquad
\sigma^2 \sim \text{IG}(\alpha_0, \delta_0), \qquad
\nu - 2 \sim \text{Exp}(1/\bar\nu)\ \text{truncated to } (0, 48],
$$

with $m_0 = 0$, $s_0 = 0.01$, $\alpha_0 = 3$, $\delta_0 = 0.0032$ and $\bar\nu = 10$.
The prior on $\mu$ is centred at zero with a monthly standard deviation of one
percent, agnostic about the sign of the premium but ruling out absurd values. The
inverse-Gamma prior, in the Lecture 2 parameterisation implemented as
`scipy.stats.invgamma(a=alpha_0, scale=delta_0)`, has mean
$\delta_0/(\alpha_0 - 1) = 0.0016$, a monthly scale of four percent, and a shape of
three keeps it loose. The prior on $\nu$ is an exponential with mean $10$ shifted to
live on $(2, 50]$: the shift makes it proper and keeps the return variance finite,
and the truncation keeps $\nu$ where the data can speak, since the likelihood is
nearly flat beyond that point.

### Result R-3.1: every summary is a ratio of kernel integrals, and quadrature costs $G^k$

Write the prior density as $\phi(\theta)$, the likelihood as $f(y \mid \theta)$ and
the marginal likelihood as $f(y)$. Bayes theorem gives

$$
\phi(\theta \mid y) = \frac{\phi(\theta) f(y \mid \theta)}{f(y)}
\;\propto\; \phi(\theta) f(y \mid \theta) \;\equiv\; \kappa(\theta \mid y),
$$

where $\kappa(\theta \mid y)$ is a kernel of the posterior, the shape of a density
with the normalising constant left out. Any posterior summary is the expectation of
some function $g(\theta)$, and written with the kernel it becomes

$$
\mathbb{E}[g(\theta) \mid y]
= \int g(\theta)\, \phi(\theta \mid y)\, d\theta
= \frac{\displaystyle\int g(\theta)\, \kappa(\theta \mid y)\, d\theta}
       {\displaystyle\int \kappa(\theta \mid y)\, d\theta},
$$

because multiplying numerator and denominator by the same missing constant
$K(y) = \int \kappa(\theta \mid y)\, d\theta$ leaves the ratio unchanged, and the
denominator is the special case $g(\theta) = 1$. For this model neither integral has
a closed form. Lecture 2 could evaluate both because the exponent of its likelihood
was a quadratic form in $\beta$ and a power of $\sigma^2$, so a conjugate prior
returned a recognisable kernel; here $\nu$ enters through $\Gamma(\nu/2)$ and through
an exponent that depends on it, no finite-dimensional sufficient statistic exists,
and no conjugate family for $\nu$ is available at all. The general fallback is
deterministic quadrature, and it carries its own bound: a product rule with $G$ points
per coordinate needs $G^{k}$ evaluations of $\kappa$, so the cost is exponential in
the number of parameters.

Two different failures are packed into that statement and it is worth keeping them
apart. The first is that $K(y)$ itself has no closed form, so we know only the kernel;
the ratio above dispatches exactly that, since it never asks for $K(y)$ separately.
The second is that even with a fully known density a particular $g$ may have no
closed-form integral, as with a ratio of two jointly Normal parameters, a well defined
random variable that can nonetheless fail to have a finite mean, exactly as Lecture 2
warned when dividing one regression coefficient by another. Both occur here, and the
methods of @sec-methodology handle both at once.

The kernel itself is available in closed form and cheap to evaluate. We code its
logarithm, because the likelihood of $439$ observations is of order $e^{750}$ and
would overflow otherwise. With $k = 3$ we can still afford the brute-force answer, and
it is worth buying once: a product grid gives a reference value for every quantity in
the chapter, so each simulation method below can be checked rather than trusted.

```{python}
m_0, s_0 = 0.0, 0.01                    # mu ~ N(m_0, s_0^2)
alpha_0, delta_0 = 3.0, 0.0032          # sigma^2 ~ IG(alpha_0, delta_0)
nu_lo, nu_hi, nu_mean = 2.0, 50.0, 10.0 # nu - 2 ~ Exp(1/nu_mean) truncated to (0, 48]
nu_const = -np.log(nu_mean) - np.log(1.0 - np.exp(-(nu_hi - nu_lo) / nu_mean))


def log_prior(mu, sigma, nu):
    """Log joint prior density of (mu, sigma, nu); sigma carries the IG Jacobian 2*sigma."""
    lp = -0.5 * np.log(2 * np.pi * s_0 ** 2) - 0.5 * ((mu - m_0) / s_0) ** 2
    lp = lp + (np.log(2.0 * sigma) + alpha_0 * np.log(delta_0) - gammaln(alpha_0)
               - (alpha_0 + 1) * np.log(sigma ** 2) - delta_0 / sigma ** 2)
    return lp + nu_const - (nu - nu_lo) / nu_mean


def log_lik(mu, sigma, nu):
    """Student-t log likelihood, evaluated in blocks to bound memory."""
    out = np.empty(mu.shape)
    for i in range(0, mu.size, 20_000):
        m, s, v = mu[i:i + 20_000], sigma[i:i + 20_000], nu[i:i + 20_000]
        z2 = ((r[None, :] - m[:, None]) / s[:, None]) ** 2
        out[i:i + 20_000] = (n * (gammaln((v + 1) / 2) - gammaln(v / 2)
                                  - 0.5 * np.log(np.pi * v) - np.log(s))
                             - 0.5 * (v + 1) * np.log1p(z2 / v[:, None]).sum(axis=1))
    return out


def log_kernel(mu, sigma, nu):
    """log kappa(theta | y), minus infinity outside the prior support."""
    mu, sigma, nu = (np.asarray(a, float).ravel()
                     for a in np.broadcast_arrays(mu, sigma, nu))
    out = np.full(mu.shape, -np.inf)
    ok = (sigma > 0) & (nu > nu_lo) & (nu <= nu_hi)
    if ok.any():
        out[ok] = log_lik(mu[ok], sigma[ok], nu[ok]) + log_prior(mu[ok], sigma[ok], nu[ok])
    return out


g_mu = np.linspace(0.0015, 0.017, 64)
g_sig = np.linspace(0.029, 0.049, 64)
g_nu = np.linspace(2.02, 50.0, 96)
MU, SG, NU = np.meshgrid(g_mu, g_sig, g_nu, indexing="ij")

log_k_grid = log_kernel(MU, SG, NU).reshape(MU.shape)
p_grid = np.exp(log_k_grid - log_k_grid.max())
p_grid /= p_grid.sum()

grid_mean = np.array([(p_grid * MU).sum(), (p_grid * SG).sum(), (p_grid * NU).sum()])
grid_sd = np.array([np.sqrt((p_grid * MU ** 2).sum() - grid_mean[0] ** 2),
                    np.sqrt((p_grid * SG ** 2).sum() - grid_mean[1] ** 2),
                    np.sqrt((p_grid * NU ** 2).sum() - grid_mean[2] ** 2)])
names = ["mu", "sigma", "nu"]
print(f"log kappa at (0.009, 0.038, 8) = {log_kernel(0.009, 0.038, 8.0)[0]:.3f}")
print(f"grid evaluations: {MU.size:,}")
for nm, m_, s_ in zip(names, grid_mean, grid_sd):
    print(f"grid posterior  E[{nm:>5s} | r] = {m_:9.6f}   sd = {s_:.6f}")
print(f"annualised premium at the posterior mean: {12 * grid_mean[0]:.4f}")
print(f"implied return sd {grid_mean[1]*np.sqrt(grid_mean[2]/(grid_mean[2]-2)):.4f} "
      f"monthly vs sample sd {r.std(ddof=1):.4f}")

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(10.5, 3.4))
for ax, Xg, axis_keep, gr, nm, lab in [
        (axes[0], MU, (1, 2), g_mu, grid_mean[0], r"$\mu$  (monthly premium)"),
        (axes[1], SG, (0, 2), g_sig, grid_mean[1], r"$\sigma$  (monthly scale)"),
        (axes[2], NU, (0, 1), g_nu, grid_mean[2], r"$\nu$  (degrees of freedom)")]:
    marg = p_grid.sum(axis=axis_keep)
    ax.plot(gr, marg / np.trapezoid(marg, gr), color="steelblue")
    ax.axvline(nm, color="grey", ls=":")
    ax.set_xlabel(lab); ax.set_ylabel("density")
axes[2].set_xlim(2, 30)
fig.suptitle("The target posterior: marginals from a 393,216-point grid")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

The posterior mean premium is $0.9126\%$ a month, or $10.95\%$ a year, noticeably
above the sample average of $0.745\%$ a month that @sec-motivation reported. That gap
is the Student $t$ at work: a Normal model has to explain the 2008 and 2020 crashes by
lowering the mean, while the $t$ model reads them as tail draws and leaves the central
tendency higher. The posterior mean scale is $0.03776$ and the posterior mean degrees
of freedom is $8.60$ with a posterior standard deviation of $3.93$, so the marginal for
$\nu$ is wide and clearly right-skewed. The implied monthly return standard deviation is
$0.0431$ against a sample value of $0.0439$, so the model is not buying fat tails at the
cost of overall spread.

The number to keep from this section is not any of those, however, but $393{,}216$, the
count of kernel evaluations the grid cost at $64 \times 64 \times 96$ points. Result
R-3.1 says that count is $G^k$. At the same resolution a five-parameter version of this
model would need about $10^{9}$ evaluations and a ten-parameter one about $10^{18}$.
Grids answer this question and then stop working, permanently, one or two parameters
later. The right-skewness of the $\nu$ marginal is worth noticing now too, because it is
what breaks the first simulation method we try.

## Methodology: Monte Carlo, importance sampling and rejection {#sec-methodology}

Every method below replaces the ratio of Result R-3.1 by an average over draws. They
differ in where the draws come from and in what has to be done to them afterwards.

### Result R-3.2: the Monte Carlo estimator, its unbiasedness and its standard error

Let $\theta^{(1)}, \dots, \theta^{(S)}$ be independent draws from a distribution $p$ on
$\mathbb{R}^k$, and let $g: \mathbb{R}^k \to \mathbb{R}$ have
$\mathbb{E}_p[g(\theta)] = \mu_g$ and
$\operatorname{Var}_p[g(\theta)] = \sigma_g^2 < \infty$. The Monte Carlo estimator

$$
\hat g_S = \frac{1}{S}\sum_{s=1}^{S} g\big(\theta^{(s)}\big)
$$

satisfies, for every $S$ and every dimension $k$,

$$
\mathbb{E}\big[\hat g_S\big] = \mu_g, \qquad
\operatorname{Var}\big[\hat g_S\big] = \frac{\sigma_g^2}{S}, \qquad
\hat g_S \overset{\text{a.s.}}{\longrightarrow} \mu_g, \qquad
\sqrt{S}\,(\hat g_S - \mu_g) \overset{d}{\longrightarrow} \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_g^2).
$$

The Monte Carlo standard error is $\text{MCSE} = \sigma_g/\sqrt{S}$, estimated in
practice by $\hat\sigma_g/\sqrt{S}$ with $\hat\sigma_g$ the sample standard deviation of
the $g(\theta^{(s)})$.

Nothing in that statement mentions $k$. That is why simulation escapes the curse of
dimensionality that sank the grid in Result R-3.1: the accuracy of $\hat g_S$ depends on
the variability of the single random variable $g(\theta)$, not on the volume of the space
$\theta$ lives in. The $\sqrt{S}$ in the denominator is the compensating bad news and the
single most important practical fact about simulation. The error shrinks with the square
root of the number of draws, so halving the standard error costs four times as many draws
and one extra decimal digit costs a hundred times as many. Every later question of the
form "how many draws do we need" comes back to this line.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Derivation

Unbiasedness is linearity of expectation together with the fact that each $\theta^{(s)}$
is a draw from $p$:

$$
\mathbb{E}\big[\hat g_S\big]
= \frac{1}{S}\sum_{s=1}^S \mathbb{E}\big[g(\theta^{(s)})\big]
= \frac{1}{S}\sum_{s=1}^S \mathbb{E}_p[g(\theta)] = \mu_g .
$$

Each term is a scalar expectation, so the argument is indifferent to how many components
$\theta$ has.

For the variance, the terms $g(\theta^{(1)}), \dots, g(\theta^{(S)})$ are independent and
identically distributed, so the variance of a sum is the sum of the variances:

$$
\operatorname{Var}\big[\hat g_S\big]
= \frac{1}{S^2}\sum_{s=1}^S \operatorname{Var}\big[g(\theta^{(s)})\big]
= \frac{1}{S^2}\, S\, \sigma_g^2 = \frac{\sigma_g^2}{S}.
$$

Consistency is the strong law of large numbers applied to the one-dimensional sequence
$g(\theta^{(1)}), g(\theta^{(2)}), \dots$, which is a sequence of numbers whatever the
dimension of the object that produced them. The limiting Normality is the central limit
theorem applied to that same sequence, which is legitimate precisely because $\hat g_S$
is itself an average of independent, identically distributed terms of finite variance.
Replacing $\sigma_g$ by its sample counterpart is justified by Slutsky's theorem, since
$\hat\sigma_g \to \sigma_g$ almost surely.
:::

All of that assumes we can draw from the distribution we are integrating against. For a
prior we usually can; for a posterior known only up to a constant and belonging to no
named family, no generator exists. The next two results are the standard ways around
that.

### Result R-3.3: importance sampling, the self-normalised estimator and the effective sample size

The idea is to rewrite the target expectation as an expectation under a distribution we
can sample, called the proposal or importance density $q$, by multiplying and dividing
inside the integral. Let $p$ be a density on $\mathbb{R}^k$ and let $q$ be a density with
$q(\theta) > 0$ wherever $g(\theta) p(\theta) \neq 0$. Then

$$
\mathbb{E}_p[g(\theta)]
= \int g(\theta)\, \frac{p(\theta)}{q(\theta)}\, q(\theta)\, d\theta
= \mathbb{E}_q\big[g(\theta)\, w(\theta)\big],
\qquad w(\theta) = \frac{p(\theta)}{q(\theta)},
$$

exactly, not approximately. If $p$ is known only through a kernel
$\kappa(\theta) = c\, p(\theta)$ with $c$ unknown, then with
$\tilde w^{(s)} = \kappa(\theta^{(s)})/q(\theta^{(s)})$ and
$\theta^{(1)},\dots,\theta^{(S)} \overset{\text{iid}}{\sim} q$ the self-normalised
estimator

$$
\hat g_S^{\,\text{IS}}
= \frac{\sum_{s=1}^{S} g(\theta^{(s)})\, \tilde w^{(s)}}{\sum_{s=1}^{S} \tilde w^{(s)}}
= \sum_{s=1}^{S} g(\theta^{(s)})\, w_{\text{norm}}^{(s)},
\qquad w_{\text{norm}}^{(s)} = \frac{\tilde w^{(s)}}{\sum_{j} \tilde w^{(j)}},
$$

is biased for every finite $S$, with bias of order $1/S$, but is consistent and
asymptotically Normal at rate $\sqrt{S}$. Its variance is governed by the weights: the
second moment of a single weighted term is
$\mathbb{E}_q[\{g(\theta)w(\theta)\}^2] = \mathbb{E}_p[g(\theta)^2 w(\theta)]$, so the
variance is inflated exactly where $w(\theta)$ is large and $g(\theta)^2 p(\theta)$ is
not negligible, and if $q$ has lighter tails than $p$ in some direction then
$w(\theta) \to \infty$ along it and the variance can be infinite even though the
estimator remains consistent. The standard one-number diagnostic is the effective sample
size

$$
\text{ESS} = \frac{\big(\sum_{s} \tilde w^{(s)}\big)^2}{\sum_{s} (\tilde w^{(s)})^2}
= \frac{1}{\sum_{s} \big(w_{\text{norm}}^{(s)}\big)^2} \;\in\; [1, S],
$$

which equals $S$ when all normalised weights are $1/S$ and falls towards $1$ as a single
weight comes to dominate. It is the number of independent draws from $p$ that the
weighted sample is worth.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Derivation

The identity is a change of measure. Multiplying and dividing the integrand by $q(\theta)$
is legitimate wherever $q(\theta) > 0$, and the support condition guarantees that the set
where $q(\theta) = 0$ contributes nothing to $\int g p$. Recognising
$g(\theta)\{p(\theta)/q(\theta)\}$ as a function integrated against the density $q$ gives
$\mathbb{E}_q[g w]$. For the self-normalised version, write

$$
\hat A_S = \frac{1}{S}\sum_{s=1}^S g(\theta^{(s)})\, w(\theta^{(s)}), \qquad
\hat B_S = \frac{1}{S}\sum_{s=1}^S w(\theta^{(s)}),
$$

where $w = p/q$ is the weight built from the normalised $p$. Each is an ordinary Monte
Carlo average of independent draws from $q$, so by Result R-3.2 $\hat A_S$ is unbiased
and consistent for $\mathbb{E}_q[gw] = \mathbb{E}_p[g]$ and $\hat B_S$ for
$\mathbb{E}_q[w] = \int p = 1$.

The unknown constant $c$ multiplies every $\tilde w^{(s)}$ identically, so it cancels from
the ratio and $\hat g_S^{\,\text{IS}} = \hat A_S / \hat B_S$ exactly. This is where
unbiasedness is lost: the expectation of a ratio is not the ratio of expectations, because
$1/\hat B_S$ is convex in $\hat B_S$ and Jensen's inequality bites. A second-order
expansion of $\hat A_S/\hat B_S$ around $(\mathbb{E}\hat A_S, 1)$ gives

$$
\mathbb{E}\big[\hat g_S^{\,\text{IS}}\big] - \mu_g
= \frac{1}{S}\Big\{\mu_g \operatorname{Var}_q[w] - \operatorname{Cov}_q[gw,\, w]\Big\}
+ O(S^{-2}),
$$

so the bias is of order $1/S$ and vanishes faster than the standard error, which is of
order $S^{-1/2}$.

Consistency survives intact. Both $\hat A_S$ and $\hat B_S$ converge almost surely by the
law of large numbers, $\hat B_S \to 1 \neq 0$, and the map $(a, b) \mapsto a/b$ is
continuous there, so the continuous mapping theorem gives
$\hat g_S^{\,\text{IS}} \to \mu_g/1$ almost surely. The delta method applied to the same
ratio gives $\sqrt{S}(\hat g_S^{\,\text{IS}} - \mu_g) \overset{d}{\to}
\mathcal{N}(0, \tau_g^2)$ with $\tau_g^2 = \operatorname{Var}_q[w(\theta)\{g(\theta) -
\mu_g\}]$, provided that variance is finite. Notice that $\tau_g^2$ involves the weights
quadratically, which is the formal reason uneven weights are expensive.

The second-moment identity is the same change of measure applied to $g^2 w^2$ rather than
to $g w$: one factor of $q$ in the denominator cancels against the $q$ from the
expectation, leaving $g^2 w$ integrated against $p$. Subtracting $\mu_g^2$ gives the
variance of a single term, and dividing by $S$ gives the variance of the estimator.

For the effective sample size, compare the variance of the weighted average with that of
an unweighted average of $S_{\text{eff}}$ draws from $p$. Treating the weights as fixed,
$\sum_s w_{\text{norm}}^{(s)} g(\theta^{(s)})$ has variance
$\sigma_g^2 \sum_s (w_{\text{norm}}^{(s)})^2$, while the unweighted average has variance
$\sigma_g^2/S_{\text{eff}}$. Equating them gives
$S_{\text{eff}} = 1/\sum_s (w_{\text{norm}}^{(s)})^2$. The bounds follow from
$\sum_s (w_{\text{norm}}^{(s)})^2 \ge 1/S$ by Cauchy-Schwarz, with equality when all
weights are equal, and $\le 1$, with equality when one weight is one and the rest zero.
:::

The practical reading is unglamorous but important. The bias shrinks like $1/S$ while the
spread shrinks like $S^{-1/2}$, so the bias is asymptotically negligible relative to the
noise, but no single run at small $S$ is guaranteed to sit on the truth. The trade is
worth making because working with an unnormalised target is usually the only option.

One technical point saves confusion later. Everything above used a normalised $q$, but in
practice one often knows only a kernel $\iota(\theta) \propto q(\theta)$ with unknown
constant $c_\iota = \int \iota$. Building the weight from $\iota$ changes every weight by
the same factor $c_\iota$, which cancels in the self-normalised ratio, so
$\hat g_S^{\,\text{IS}}$ is unaffected. What changes is that the raw average of such
weights no longer estimates one; it estimates $K(y)/c_\iota$. When $c_\iota$ is known,
that average times $c_\iota$ is therefore an estimator of the marginal likelihood $K(y)$,
which is how Lecture 9 computes model evidence.

Every requirement on a good proposal follows from keeping $w = \kappa/q$ well behaved: its
support must cover everywhere the target has mass, its tails must be no lighter than the
target's, since a proposal that decays faster sends $w \to \infty$ in the tail, and it
must be cheap to sample. One construction is safe by arithmetic rather than by inspection.
Because the likelihood is bounded above by some finite $\bar l$, the kernel obeys
$\kappa(\theta) = l(\theta)\phi(\theta) \le \bar l\, \phi(\theta)$, so a proposal built
from the prior can never have lighter tails than the posterior.

### Exact draws by rejection

Importance sampling returns weighted points. Rejection sampling returns actual draws from
the target, by discarding proposals geometrically rather than reweighting them. Let
$\kappa$ be a kernel of the target with $K = \int \kappa(\theta)\, d\theta < \infty$ and
target density $p = \kappa/K$, and let $q$ be a density and $M$ a constant with
$\kappa(\theta) \le M\, q(\theta)$ for all $\theta$. Repeat: draw $\tilde\theta \sim q$ and
$u \sim \text{Uniform}(0,1)$ independently, and accept $\theta = \tilde\theta$ if

$$
u \le \frac{\kappa(\tilde\theta)}{M\, q(\tilde\theta)} ,
$$

otherwise discard and start again. Then every accepted $\theta$ is an exact draw from $p$,
accepted draws are mutually independent, and the acceptance probability at any single
trial is $\Pr(\text{accept}) = K/M$, so the expected number of proposals per accepted draw
is $M/K$. No reweighting of accepted draws is needed, which is the advantage; finding a
valid $M$ is the price.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Derivation

Take the joint density of proposing $\tilde\theta$ and accepting it. The proposal has
density $q(\theta)$, and given $\tilde\theta = \theta$ the acceptance event has
probability $\kappa(\theta)/\{M q(\theta)\}$ because $u$ is uniform on $(0,1)$ and the
envelope condition guarantees the ratio lies in $[0,1]$. Hence

$$
\Pr(\text{propose near }\theta \text{ and accept})
= q(\theta)\, \frac{\kappa(\theta)}{M q(\theta)} = \frac{\kappa(\theta)}{M} .
$$

Integrating over $\theta$ gives the unconditional acceptance probability
$\int \kappa(\theta)\, d\theta / M = K/M$. Dividing the joint density by that probability
gives the density of an accepted draw,

$$
p(\theta \mid \text{accept}) = \frac{\kappa(\theta)/M}{K/M}
= \frac{\kappa(\theta)}{K} = p(\theta),
$$

which is the target exactly, with the unknown constant $K$ cancelling. Independence of
successive accepted draws follows because the trials are independent and the accept
decision depends only on the current trial.

Geometrically the same argument reads as an area statement. The first two steps generate a
point uniformly over the region under the envelope,
$\{(\theta, v) : 0 \le v \le M q(\theta)\}$, since $\theta$ comes from $q$ and
$v = u M q(\theta)$ is uniform on $[0, M q(\theta)]$ given $\theta$. The third keeps the
points that also fall under $\kappa$, a sub-region of the envelope. A point uniform on a
region and restricted to a sub-region is uniform on that sub-region, and the marginal of
$\theta$ under a uniform distribution on the area beneath a curve is the density
proportional to that curve. The acceptance probability is the ratio of the two areas, and
when $q = p$ exactly $M = 1$ and everything is accepted.
:::

One special case deserves naming because it recurs throughout the course. Suppose the
target is an unrestricted posterior with kernel $\kappa(\theta)$ truncated to a region
$\Theta_r$, and the unrestricted posterior is already easy to simulate. Then it serves as
its own proposal with envelope constant exactly $M = 1$, since
$\kappa(\theta)\mathbf{1}\{\theta \in \Theta_r\} \le 1 \cdot \kappa(\theta)$ holds
trivially, and the algorithm collapses to drawing from the unrestricted posterior and
discarding whatever falls outside $\Theta_r$. The acceptance rate is then
$\Pr(\theta \in \Theta_r \mid y)$, usually a quantity of interest in its own right. This is
how sign restrictions are imposed in the structural vector autoregressions of Lecture 7.

### Turning weights into draws: sampling importance resampling

Between the two lies a cheap compromise. Having drawn
$\theta^{(1)}, \dots, \theta^{(S)} \sim q$ with normalised weights $w_{\text{norm}}^{(s)}$,
draw $N \le S$ indices from $\{1, \dots, S\}$ with replacement using the weights as
selection probabilities and keep the corresponding $\theta$ values. A heavily weighted draw
is copied more often and a negligible one is unlikely to appear, so the resampled set is
approximately an unweighted sample from $p$. The approximation is exact only as
$S \to \infty$ with $N$ fixed, which is the essential difference from rejection sampling,
but it needs no envelope constant and wastes no draws.

## Data: monthly US market excess returns, 1990 to 2026 {#sec-data}

The chapter's dataset is the monthly Fama-French factor file,
`data/ff_factors_monthly.parquet`, from the Kenneth French data library, and the single
column used is `mkt_rf`, the excess return on the value-weighted US market portfolio over
the one-month Treasury bill. The window is January 1990 to July 2026, which is $439$
complete months and the same window Lecture 2 used for the banking regression, so the two
chapters describe the same regime. Chapters 4 and 5 reuse this series, this window and this
model without change, so that every sampler in the course can be compared on one problem
rather than on five.

```{python}
print(f"{n} months, {sample.index[0]:%Y-%m} to {sample.index[-1]:%Y-%m}")
print(f"mean {r.mean():.5f}  sd {r.std(ddof=1):.5f}  "
      f"skewness {stats.skew(r):.3f}  kurtosis {stats.kurtosis(r, fisher=False):.3f}")
print(f"five worst months: {np.sort(r)[:5].round(3)}")

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9.5, 3.6))
axes[0].plot(sample.index, r, lw=0.8, color="steelblue")
axes[0].set_xlabel("date"); axes[0].set_ylabel("monthly excess return")
axes[0].set_title(f"Market excess return, {n} months")
grid_r = np.linspace(-0.20, 0.20, 400)
axes[1].hist(r, bins=40, density=True, alpha=0.55, color="steelblue", label="data")
axes[1].plot(grid_r, stats.norm(r.mean(), r.std(ddof=1)).pdf(grid_r), "k--",
             lw=1.5, label="fitted Normal")
axes[1].set_xlabel("monthly excess return"); axes[1].set_ylabel("density")
axes[1].legend(fontsize=9); axes[1].set_title("Tails are thicker than Normal")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

The series has a mean of $0.00745$ and a standard deviation of $0.04392$ a month, so the
average month earns three quarters of a percent over the bill rate with a typical swing
about six times that size. The skewness is $-0.545$ and the kurtosis $4.026$ against the
Normal's $3$, and the five worst months are losses of $17.2\%$, $16.0\%$, $13.4\%$,
$10.7\%$ and $10.3\%$, all of which are the numbers the model of @sec-problem is being
asked to accommodate.

The left panel shows the familiar clusters of turbulence around 2000, 2008 and 2020. That
clustering is visible enough to be worth naming as a known defect of the model rather than
a discovery: the specification treats the $439$ months as independent and identically
distributed, so it can accommodate a fat tail but not a tail that arrives in bursts, and
@sec-discussion returns to the point. The right panel is the reason for the model in the
first place. The histogram has more mass than the fitted Normal in the centre and in the
far tails and less in the shoulders, which is the signature of a scale mixture rather than
of a single Gaussian, and the Student $t$ is the simplest distribution with that shape.

## Empirical analysis: three simulators on one Student-$t$ posterior {#sec-empirical}

The three methods of @sec-methodology are now run on the posterior of @sec-problem, in
the order in which a working paper would report them: first Monte Carlo where the answer
is known exactly, so that the standard error can be audited; then importance sampling
twice, once with the obvious proposal and once with a proposal chosen to have heavy
tails; then rejection sampling, which delivers exact draws; and finally resampling, which
converts a weighted sample into an unweighted one. Every estimate is compared against the
$393{,}216$-point grid, which is available here and will not be available again after
Lecture 5.

### Monte Carlo where the answer is known

To see Result R-3.2 work before the difficulty arrives, apply it to the one distribution in
this model we can sample directly, the prior, two of whose moments are known exactly:
$\mathbb{E}[\sigma^2] = \delta_0/(\alpha_0 - 1) = 0.0016$, and for the truncated shifted
exponential with rate $\lambda = 1/\bar\nu$ on $(2, 2+b]$,
$\mathbb{E}[\nu] = 2 + 1/\lambda - b e^{-\lambda b}/(1 - e^{-\lambda b})$. Drawing from the
prior on $\nu$ uses the inverse transform,
$\nu = 2 - \bar\nu \log\{1 - u(1 - e^{-b/\bar\nu})\}$ with $u$ uniform.

```{python}
S_mc = 20_000
mu_pr = rng.normal(m_0, s_0, size=S_mc)
sig_pr = np.sqrt(stats.invgamma(a=alpha_0, scale=delta_0).rvs(size=S_mc, random_state=rng))
u_pr = rng.uniform(size=S_mc)
b_nu = nu_hi - nu_lo
nu_pr = nu_lo - nu_mean * np.log(1.0 - u_pr * (1.0 - np.exp(-b_nu / nu_mean)))

exact_var = delta_0 / (alpha_0 - 1.0)
exact_nu = nu_lo + nu_mean - b_nu * np.exp(-b_nu / nu_mean) / (1 - np.exp(-b_nu / nu_mean))

for lab, draws, exact in [("E[sigma^2]", sig_pr ** 2, exact_var),
                          ("E[nu]      ", nu_pr, exact_nu)]:
    est = draws.mean()
    mcse = draws.std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(S_mc)
    print(f"prior {lab}  exact {exact:10.6f}   MC {est:10.6f}   "
          f"MCSE {mcse:.6f}   |error|/MCSE {abs(est - exact) / mcse:.2f}")

run_est = np.cumsum(nu_pr) / np.arange(1, S_mc + 1)
s_axis = np.arange(1, S_mc + 1)
band = 1.96 * nu_pr.std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(s_axis)

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(s_axis, run_est, lw=1, color="steelblue", label="running MC estimate")
ax.axhline(exact_nu, color="black", lw=1, ls=":", label="exact prior mean")
ax.fill_between(s_axis, exact_nu - band, exact_nu + band, alpha=0.2,
                label=r"exact $\pm\,1.96\times$MCSE")
ax.set_xscale("log")
ax.set_xlabel("number of draws  S (log scale)"); ax.set_ylabel(r"estimate of $E[\nu]$")
ax.set_ylim(exact_nu - 2, exact_nu + 2)
ax.legend(); ax.set_title(r"Monte Carlo error shrinks like $1/\sqrt{S}$")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

Both estimates sit within two Monte Carlo standard errors of the exact value, which is what
an unbiased estimator with a correctly computed standard error should do. That standard
error says nothing about the prior, which is fixed; it says how far this particular average
of $20{,}000$ draws might be from the number the draws estimate. The band in the figure
narrows steadily and the running average stays inside it without ever settling on the exact
value, which is Result R-3.2 made concrete. Note how slow the narrowing is on the
logarithmic axis: each factor of ten in $S$ buys a factor of only about three in accuracy.

### A Normal proposal, and why it fails

For the posterior the natural first attempt at a proposal is a Normal centred at the mode
with covariance taken from the curvature of the log kernel there, the Laplace approximation,
inflated a little for safety.

```{python}
neg_log_kernel = lambda t: -log_kernel(t[0], t[1], t[2])[0]
opt = optimize.minimize(neg_log_kernel, np.array([0.009, 0.038, 8.0]),
                        method="Nelder-Mead",
                        options=dict(xatol=1e-8, fatol=1e-8, maxiter=5000))
theta_hat = opt.x

step = np.array([1e-4, 1e-4, 1e-2])                  # central second differences
H = np.empty((3, 3))
for i in range(3):
    for j in range(3):
        ei, ej = np.zeros(3), np.zeros(3)
        ei[i], ej[j] = step[i], step[j]
        H[i, j] = (neg_log_kernel(theta_hat + ei + ej) - neg_log_kernel(theta_hat + ei - ej)
                   - neg_log_kernel(theta_hat - ei + ej)
                   + neg_log_kernel(theta_hat - ei - ej)) / (4 * step[i] * step[j])
Sigma_hat = np.linalg.inv(H)

print(f"posterior mode:  mu {theta_hat[0]:.6f}  sigma {theta_hat[1]:.6f}  nu {theta_hat[2]:.4f}")
print("Laplace sd:     " + "  ".join(f"{v:.6f}" for v in np.sqrt(np.diag(Sigma_hat))))

S_is = 40_000
q_normal = stats.multivariate_normal(mean=theta_hat, cov=4.0 * Sigma_hat)   # scale inflated 2x
th_n = q_normal.rvs(size=S_is, random_state=rng)

log_w = log_kernel(th_n[:, 0], th_n[:, 1], th_n[:, 2]) - q_normal.logpdf(th_n)
w_n = np.where(np.isfinite(log_w), np.exp(log_w - log_w[np.isfinite(log_w)].max()), 0.0)
w_n /= w_n.sum()

ess_n = 1.0 / np.sum(w_n ** 2)
is_mean_n = w_n @ th_n
print(f"outside the prior support: {np.mean(~np.isfinite(log_w)):.3f} of draws")
for nm, est, tru in zip(names, is_mean_n, grid_mean):
    print(f"IS(Normal)  E[{nm:>5s}] = {est:9.6f}   grid {tru:9.6f}   "
          f"error {est - tru:+.6f}")
print(f"ESS = {ess_n:.0f} out of {S_is} ({100*ess_n/S_is:.1f}%), "
      f"largest normalised weight {w_n.max():.4f}")
```

The estimates for $\mu$ and $\sigma$ are excellent, agreeing with the grid to within a few
parts in ten thousand. The estimate for $\nu$ is not: it comes out at $8.42$ against the
grid value of $8.60$, an error of two percent that no amount of staring at the point
estimate would reveal. The effective sample size of Result R-3.3 explains why. It is about
eight percent of the draws, and the diagnosis follows from the shape of the posterior: the
marginal for $\nu$ is right-skewed with a long tail towards thirty, while a Normal
proposal's tail dies like $e^{-x^2}$. In the region $\nu \in (15, 40)$, where the posterior
still has real mass, the proposal has almost none, so the few draws that land there carry
very large weights, and a right tail represented by a handful of heavy points is a right
tail estimated badly. Thirteen percent of the proposal's draws land outside the prior
support altogether, at negative $\sigma$ or at $\nu$ below $2$, and are wasted outright.

### A heavy-tailed proposal

The repair is to give the proposal heavier tails than the target in every direction, built
component by component: a Student $t_5$ for $\mu$ and for $\sigma$, whose polynomial tails
dominate the posterior's exponential ones, and for $\nu$ the prior itself, which by the
boundedness argument of @sec-methodology can never have lighter tails than the posterior.

```{python}
q_mu = stats.t(df=5, loc=0.00913, scale=0.0022)
q_sig = stats.t(df=5, loc=0.0378, scale=0.0024)
q_nu = stats.truncexpon(b=(nu_hi - nu_lo) / nu_mean, loc=nu_lo, scale=nu_mean)


def q_rvs(size, generator):
    return np.column_stack([q_mu.rvs(size, random_state=generator),
                            q_sig.rvs(size, random_state=generator),
                            q_nu.rvs(size, random_state=generator)])


def q_logpdf(th):
    return q_mu.logpdf(th[:, 0]) + q_sig.logpdf(th[:, 1]) + q_nu.logpdf(th[:, 2])


th_h = q_rvs(S_is, rng)
log_w_h = log_kernel(th_h[:, 0], th_h[:, 1], th_h[:, 2]) - q_logpdf(th_h)
w_h = np.where(np.isfinite(log_w_h),
               np.exp(log_w_h - log_w_h[np.isfinite(log_w_h)].max()), 0.0)
w_h /= w_h.sum()

ess_h = 1.0 / np.sum(w_h ** 2)
is_mean_h = w_h @ th_h
for nm, est, tru in zip(names, is_mean_h, grid_mean):
    print(f"IS(heavy)   E[{nm:>5s}] = {est:9.6f}   grid {tru:9.6f}   "
          f"error {est - tru:+.6f}")
print(f"ESS = {ess_h:.0f} out of {S_is} ({100*ess_h/S_is:.1f}%), "
      f"largest normalised weight {w_h.max():.4f}")

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9.5, 3.8))
for ax, ww, ess_, ttl in [(axes[0], w_n, ess_n, "Normal proposal (Laplace, inflated)"),
                          (axes[1], w_h, ess_h, "heavy-tailed proposal")]:
    ax.hist(ww * S_is, bins=60, color="steelblue", alpha=0.85)
    ax.set_yscale("log")
    ax.set_xlabel(r"normalised weight $\times\, S$")
    ax.set_title(f"{ttl}\nESS = {ess_:.0f} of {S_is}  ({100*ess_/S_is:.1f}%)", fontsize=10)
axes[0].set_ylabel("count (log scale)")
fig.suptitle("Importance weights on the Student-t posterior")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

The heavier-tailed proposal raises the effective sample size to about thirty percent of the
draws and brings the estimate of $\nu$ to within four hundredths of the grid value. The
figure shows why. Both weight distributions are right-skewed, which is normal and not by
itself a problem; what differs is the extreme. The largest single normalised weight under
the Normal proposal is roughly five hundred times the average weight $1/S$, while under the
heavy-tailed proposal it is about eight times. A weight distribution whose maximum is far
out relative to its bulk is the visual form of a small effective sample size, and it is the
thing to look at before believing any importance sampling estimate.

Two habits keep such a run honest. Always plot the weights, and treat a single draw carrying
a large share of the total as a failure of the proposal rather than an accident of the seed.
And track the coefficient of variation of the raw weights, $\text{sd}(w)/\text{mean}(w)$, as
$S$ grows: one that keeps climbing is the signature of an infinite weight variance and cannot
be trusted however large $S$ is made.

### Exact draws, and what they cost

The envelope constant is the whole practical problem for rejection sampling. We need an
$M \ge \sup_\theta \kappa(\theta)/q(\theta)$, and we reuse the heavy-tailed proposal, whose
tails dominate the target's in every direction so that the supremum is finite. We locate it
numerically, over the evaluation grid of @sec-problem and over a large sample from $q$,
which is reliable here only because $k = 3$ and the posterior is unimodal. In higher
dimensions a numerically located envelope is a trap, and this is one reason rejection
sampling is rarely used on large models.

```{python}
grid_pts = np.column_stack([MU.ravel(), SG.ravel(), NU.ravel()])
probe = q_rvs(300_000, rng)
log_ratio = np.concatenate([
    log_k_grid.ravel() - q_logpdf(grid_pts),
    log_kernel(probe[:, 0], probe[:, 1], probe[:, 2]) - q_logpdf(probe)])
log_M = np.nanmax(log_ratio[np.isfinite(log_ratio)])

cell = (g_mu[1] - g_mu[0]) * (g_sig[1] - g_sig[0]) * (g_nu[1] - g_nu[0])
log_K = np.log(np.exp(log_k_grid - log_k_grid.max()).sum() * cell) + log_k_grid.max()
print(f"log K (grid) = {log_K:.3f},  log M = {log_M:.3f}")
print(f"theoretical acceptance rate K/M = {np.exp(log_K - log_M):.4f}")

N_want, kept, n_tried = 20_000, [], 0
while sum(a.shape[0] for a in kept) < N_want:
    cand = q_rvs(40_000, rng)
    log_u = np.log(rng.uniform(size=cand.shape[0]))
    acc = log_u <= (log_kernel(cand[:, 0], cand[:, 1], cand[:, 2])
                    - q_logpdf(cand) - log_M)
    kept.append(cand[acc])
    n_tried += cand.shape[0]

post = np.vstack(kept)
print(f"observed acceptance rate {post.shape[0] / n_tried:.4f} "
      f"({post.shape[0]} accepted from {n_tried} proposals)")
post = post[:N_want]

for j, nm in enumerate(names):
    est, mcse = post[:, j].mean(), post[:, j].std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(N_want)
    print(f"rejection  E[{nm:>5s}] = {est:9.6f}  MCSE {mcse:.6f}  "
          f"grid {grid_mean[j]:9.6f}  |error|/MCSE {abs(est-grid_mean[j])/mcse:.2f}")
p_thick = (post[:, 2] < 10).mean()
print(f"P(nu < 10 | r) = {p_thick:.4f}  "
      f"(MCSE {np.sqrt(p_thick*(1-p_thick)/N_want):.4f})")
```

The observed acceptance rate agrees with the theoretical $K/M$ to within two
ten-thousandths, a check on both the envelope and the arithmetic, and the three posterior
means land within about one Monte Carlo standard error of the grid values. We now have
$20{,}000$ independent, unweighted draws from the posterior, usable downstream exactly like
draws from a named distribution, and they answer the strategist's other question directly:
the posterior probability that the degrees of freedom are below ten, which is to say that
the tails are genuinely thick, is $0.7567$ with a standard error of $0.0030$. The price is
the acceptance rate, roughly ten proposals per draw kept, which is tolerable here. In $k$
dimensions the volume between a safe envelope and the target typically makes $M/K$ grow
exponentially in $k$, so rejection sampling suffers from the same curse of dimensionality as
the grid of Result R-3.1, just with a slower fuse.

Two features of that printout are worth reading carefully, because they are the reason
this method is the reference for the rest of the course. The first is that the acceptance
rate is a testable prediction and not a diagnostic to be interpreted: Result R-3.3's
companion statement says it must equal $K/M$, both sides were computed by different
routes, one from a grid quadrature of the kernel and one from a Monte Carlo experiment,
and they agree to two ten-thousandths. A discrepancy there would have meant a violated
envelope condition and silently wrong draws, which is a failure mode with no other
warning sign. The second is that the accepted draws carry no weights at all, so the
standard error attached to each mean is the plain $\hat\sigma_g/\sqrt{S}$ of Result R-3.2
rather than something inflated by weight variability, and the ratios of error to standard
error, $0.51$, $0.10$ and $0.94$, are the sizes one expects from an unbiased estimator.

```{python}
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(9.5, 3.8))
marg_nu = p_grid.sum(axis=(0, 1))
axes[0].hist(post[:, 2], bins=60, density=True, alpha=0.6, color="steelblue",
             label="rejection draws")
axes[0].plot(g_nu, marg_nu / np.trapezoid(marg_nu, g_nu), "k-", lw=1.6,
             label="grid marginal")
axes[0].set_xlim(2, 30); axes[0].set_xlabel(r"$\nu$"); axes[0].set_ylabel("density")
axes[0].legend(fontsize=9); axes[0].set_title(r"Exact draws reproduce the $\nu$ marginal")
axes[1].scatter(post[:, 1], post[:, 2], s=3, alpha=0.12, color="steelblue")
axes[1].set_xlabel(r"$\sigma$"); axes[1].set_ylabel(r"$\nu$"); axes[1].set_ylim(2, 30)
axes[1].set_title(r"Joint posterior of $(\sigma, \nu)$")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

The left panel confirms that the accepted draws reproduce the grid marginal for $\nu$ with
no weight appearing anywhere in the calculation. The right panel explains the importance
sampling failure diagnosed two subsections ago: $\sigma$ and $\nu$ are strongly positively
dependent and the cloud curves upwards, because a model with thicker tails needs a smaller
scale to fit the same data. An elliptical Normal proposal cannot follow a curved ridge, so
it wastes draws on one side and starves the other.

### Resampling the weighted sample

```{python}
idx = rng.choice(S_is, size=N_want, replace=True, p=w_n)
sir = th_n[idx]
for j, nm in enumerate(names):
    print(f"SIR from the Normal proposal  E[{nm:>5s}] = {sir[:, j].mean():9.6f}   "
          f"grid {grid_mean[j]:9.6f}")
print(f"distinct source draws used: {np.unique(idx).size} of {S_is}")
```

The resampled means inherit exactly the strengths and the weakness of the weighted sample
they came from: $\mu$ and $\sigma$ are right and $\nu$ is still too low, because resampling
cannot manufacture information the proposal never collected. The number of distinct source
draws is the practical warning signal: the $20{,}000$ resampled points are built from only
$10{,}350$ distinct values, and with a badly degenerate weight distribution the same recipe
would copy a handful of dominant points over and over.

Put side by side, the four runs say the same thing about this posterior from four
directions. On $\mu$ and $\sigma$ every method is right to four significant figures,
because those two coordinates are nearly Gaussian and any reasonable proposal covers
them. On $\nu$ they separate: the grid says $8.598$, rejection sampling $8.572$ with a
standard error of $0.027$, the heavy-tailed importance sampler $8.558$, and the Normal
proposal and its resampled version $8.422$ and $8.460$. The ranking is not a ranking of
the algorithms in the abstract, since importance sampling with a good proposal beat
importance sampling with a bad one by more than rejection sampling beat either. It is a
ranking of how well each construction covered the right tail of a skewed marginal, which
is the only place the three methods could disagree. The lesson to carry forward is that
the failure was invisible in the point estimates of the other two coordinates and visible
in the effective sample size before any comparison with the grid was made.

## Discussion: value at risk, and where a fixed proposal fails {#sec-discussion}

The desk can now be answered. The equity premium is $0.91\%$ a month, or $10.95\%$ a year,
and the tails are thick with probability $0.76$. The remaining question was the loss exceeded
with probability one percent next month, and the correct object for it is the posterior
predictive distribution, which integrates over parameter uncertainty,

$$
f(r_{n+1} \mid r) = \int f(r_{n+1} \mid \theta)\, \phi(\theta \mid r)\, d\theta ,
$$

approximated by drawing one future return per posterior draw: for each accepted
$\theta^{(s)} = (\mu^{(s)}, \sigma^{(s)}, \nu^{(s)})$ take
$r_{n+1}^{(s)} = \mu^{(s)} + \sigma^{(s)} \varepsilon^{(s)}$ with
$\varepsilon^{(s)} \sim t_{\nu^{(s)}}(0,1)$. Value at risk is the empirical quantile of
those draws, which is Result R-3.2 again with $g(\theta) = \mathbf{1}\{r_{n+1} < c\}$ and
the threshold solved for. We compare three conventions: this predictive quantile, the
plug-in Student $t$ quantile that fixes $\theta$ at its posterior mean, and the Normal
convention of @sec-motivation.

```{python}
eps = stats.t(df=post[:, 2]).rvs(size=N_want, random_state=rng)
r_pred = post[:, 0] + post[:, 1] * eps

mu_b, sig_b, nu_b = post.mean(axis=0)
rows = []
for level in (0.95, 0.99, 0.995):
    a = 1 - level
    predictive = -np.quantile(r_pred, a)
    plug_t = -(mu_b + sig_b * stats.t(df=nu_b).ppf(a))
    normal = -(r.mean() + r.std(ddof=1) * stats.norm.ppf(a))
    rows.append({"level": level, "predictive": predictive, "plug-in t": plug_t,
                 "Normal": normal, "pred - plug-in": predictive - plug_t,
                 "pred - Normal": predictive - normal})
var_table = pd.DataFrame(rows).set_index("level")
print((100 * var_table).round(3).to_string() + "   (percent of notional)")
print(f"\nexpected shortfall at 99%: {-r_pred[r_pred < np.quantile(r_pred, 0.01)].mean():.4f}")
print(f"predictive sd {r_pred.std(ddof=1):.4f} vs sample sd {r.std(ddof=1):.4f}")
print(f"posterior of nu: mean {nu_b:.2f}, 2.5th percentile "
      f"{np.percentile(post[:, 2], 2.5):.2f}, 97.5th {np.percentile(post[:, 2], 97.5):.2f}")

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.hist(r_pred, bins=120, density=True, range=(-0.30, 0.25), alpha=0.55,
        color="steelblue", label="posterior predictive")
ax.hist(r, bins=40, density=True, histtype="step", lw=1.6, color="black",
        label="realised returns")
for level, colour in ((0.99, "firebrick"), (0.95, "darkorange")):
    ax.axvline(np.quantile(r_pred, 1 - level), color=colour, ls="--",
               label=f"predictive VaR {level:.0%}")
ax.set_xlabel("one-month excess return"); ax.set_ylabel("density")
ax.legend(fontsize=9); ax.set_title("Predictive distribution and value at risk")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

At the ninety-nine percent level the predictive value at risk is $10.35\%$ of notional, the
plug-in Student $t$ figure is $9.85\%$ and the Normal figure is $9.47\%$. The Normal
convention gives the smallest number because it has no tail to speak of, and the $0.87$
percentage point gap to the predictive answer is the cost of pretending the four worst months
of @sec-motivation were not there. The plug-in Student $t$ sits between: it has the fat tail,
but it fixes $\nu$ at its posterior mean of $8.57$ and ignores the posterior's own statement
that $\nu$ plausibly runs from about four to about eighteen, and it is the low end, where
the tail is heaviest, that a value at risk is sensitive to. Averaging over the posterior of
$\nu$ rather than fixing it adds the remaining half a percentage point. The gap to the
Normal convention, by contrast, grows monotonically with the level, from minus $0.23$
points at ninety-five percent to $0.87$ at ninety-nine and $1.43$ at ninety-nine and a
half, which is what it means to say that the error of a Normal model lives in the tail and
not in the middle. On a one hundred million euro book the
difference between the plug-in and the predictive number at the ninety-nine percent level
is about half a million euros of capital, which is the practical content of the phrase
"integrating over parameter uncertainty".

Two checks say the simulation can be trusted. The predictive standard deviation is $0.0441$
against a realised $0.0439$, so the fitted model reproduces the spread of the data it was
given rather than inventing tails; and every estimate in @sec-empirical was compared against
the $393{,}216$-point grid of @sec-problem, with rejection sampling landing within one Monte
Carlo standard error and the heavy-tailed importance sampler within four hundredths on the
hardest coordinate. Two qualifications belong with the number all the same. The model assumes
returns are independent and identically distributed over thirty-six years, which the
volatility clustering in the first panel of @sec-data plainly contradicts, and Lecture 12
replaces exactly this specification with stochastic volatility. And the predictive
distribution carries parameter uncertainty, not model uncertainty, which is the subject of
Lectures 9 and 11.

The binding limitation is elsewhere, and it is about the machinery rather than the model.
Everything here rested on choosing one fixed proposal $q$ in advance and using it for every
draw. Finding tails heavy enough in every direction took a few minutes of thought at $k = 3$
with a posterior we could plot and a grid to check against, and even then the first attempt
lost ninety-two percent of its draws to a curved ridge that an ellipse could not follow. That
work does not scale. As the parameter count grows the region where the posterior has mass
becomes a vanishing fraction of anything a fixed $q$ covers, the weights concentrate on a
handful of draws, and the effective sample size collapses towards one; at the $k = 40$ of
Lecture 6 no proposal chosen in advance is usable at all. Lecture 4 is the repair: instead of
one fixed proposal it writes the Student $t$ as a Normal scale mixture,
$r_t \mid \mu, \sigma, \nu, w_t \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2/w_t)$ with
$w_t \sim \text{Gamma}(\nu/2, \nu/2)$, which makes every full conditional recognisable, and
draws each block from its own conditional so that the proposal moves with the chain. Lecture
5 attacks this same posterior again without the latent variables and closes with one table of
effective sample size per second for every method in Lectures 3 to 5 on this identical
problem.

## Exercises

These are the chapter's practice questions; the [Week 3 exercise
session](../exercise-sessions/03-monte-carlo-importance-sampling.qmd) works through them and
adds the lab.

1. By hand. Derive the bias expansion of the self-normalised estimator in Result R-3.3 to
   order $1/S$, stating where Jensen's inequality enters and why the unnormalised estimator
   is exempt. Then show that for the special case $g \equiv 1$ the estimator is exactly one
   for every $S$, and explain what that says about which functions $g$ the bias can hurt.

2. Computational. Take the heavy-tailed proposal of @sec-empirical and compute the
   coefficient of variation of the raw weights at $S = 10^3, 10^4, 10^5$ and $10^6$. Repeat
   with the scale of the $\mu$ and $\sigma$ components of the proposal halved, so that its
   tails are too light. Plot both paths and say which one shows the signature of an infinite
   weight variance, then relate what you see to the effective sample sizes reported in the
   chapter.

3. On real data. Refit the model of @sec-problem to the size factor `smb` over the same
   window, keeping the priors unchanged. Report the posterior mean of $\nu$ with its Monte
   Carlo standard error, $\Pr(\nu < 10 \mid r)$, and the ninety-nine percent predictive value
   at risk, and say in one paragraph whether the size factor needs fat tails as badly as the
   market does.

Exercise 1 is the one to attempt before the session, because Lecture 9 reuses the weight
average as a marginal likelihood estimator and the same expansion controls its error.
Exercises 2 and 3 are written for the session itself and reuse the chapter's `log_kernel` and
`q_rvs` with the data line changed.

## Reading and references

The three methods of @sec-methodology follow the supplied UPM Class 3 on Monte Carlo,
importance sampling and rejection sampling, whose ordering, general statement first and one
running target afterwards, this chapter keeps. Geweke (2005), Sections 4.2 to 4.4, and
Greenberg (2008), Chapter 5, develop the integration and simulation arguments, and Greenberg
is the source for the bias expansion in the collapsed derivation of Result R-3.3. The
Student-$t$ location-scale model with unknown degrees of freedom, the target of @sec-problem,
is treated in Geweke (1993), which is also where the scale-mixture representation that
Lecture 4 exploits is set out. Robert and Casella give the rejection sampling argument in the
form used here, including the geometric reading in the collapsed derivation. The UPM materials
are by Audronė Virbickaitė and Martina Zaharieva, adapted to this course's notation and weekly
sequence.

One notational bridge is worth carrying to those sources. What this chapter calls the kernel
$\kappa(\theta \mid y)$ and the proposal $q$ appear there as $\kappa(\theta \mid y)$ and the
importance function $\iota(\theta)$, the envelope constant $M$ as $c$, and the normalising
constant $K(y)$ as the marginal likelihood $f(y)$; the inverse-Gamma prior on $\sigma^2$
appears as a Gamma prior on the precision $h = 1/\sigma^2$ with shape $\alpha_0$ and rate
$\delta_0$. The full translation table is in the week's exercise session.

The explanations and exercises are adapted to this course's notation and weekly structure;
consult the cited originals for the full treatments.

Geweke (1989). Geweke (1993), Bayesian treatment of the independent Student-$t$ linear model.
Robert and Casella, *Monte Carlo Statistical Methods*, ch. 2-3. Geweke, *Contemporary Bayesian
Econometrics and Statistics* (2005), ch. 4.
